title: A Simple Way To Calm An Excitable Class
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin identifies classroom excitability as a major driver of misbehavior and traces much of it back to the teacher's own energy, since students take their behavioral cues from the adult in the room. He offers a single, simple technique to counter it: physically slowing down. Rather than relying on willpower to overcome stress or forcing oneself to feel calmer, he draws a comparison to Tai Chi, where deliberately slower, more graceful movement naturally settles both body and mind. He explains that this deceleration does not need to be noticeable or dramatic to be effective — easing off the pace slightly deepens breathing and softens muscles, producing composure from the outside in. The technique's real power, he argues, is its contagious effect: as the teacher's calm presence spreads through the room, it quiets restlessness and restores the classroom to a more optimal state for learning.
points: Classroom excitability is largely a reflection of the teacher's own energy and stress level, since students take their cue from the adult in the room.
Slowing down physical movement calms the mind indirectly, without requiring willpower or trying to "talk yourself" into feeling calmer.
The technique is inspired by Tai Chi, where deliberate, unhurried movement naturally restores emotional equilibrium.
The pace change doesn't need to be dramatic or noticeable to students to be effective — a small ease-up is enough.
A teacher's calm, slowed presence is contagious and spreads through the classroom, settling restlessness in students as well.
quotes: Excitability is a major cause of misbehavior. Which is why it is present in virtually every classroom where the teacher is struggling.
You see, students take their cue from you. So if you’re stressed and uptight, if you’re flustered and rushing around, it will reflect in their behavior.
It’s to slow down. It’s to begin moving deliberately and gracefully. It’s to smooth out your movements, motions, and actions and downshift to a lower gear.

Those who practice Tai Chi know this phenomenon well. The very act of articulating the elegant movements of this ancient martial art has a unique way of eliminating unwanted energy and restoring emotional equilibrium.
Just ease up on your pace a little and your breathing will deepen, your muscles will soften, and you’ll begin to feel more composed and confident.
But what’s so cool about this technique is that it’s contagious. Your calm presence will spread from one student to the next and fill every corner of your classroom.
It will remove any and all disquieting feelings and usher in contentment, cooperation, and self-awareness.
